newsitem.title: USA: EIA raises US winter natgas demand, price estimates.
newsitem.headline: EIA raises US winter natgas demand, price estimates.

text.p: U.S. demand for natural gas this winter should average 72.9 billion cubic feet (bcf) per day, the Energy Information Administration said Friday, raising the estimate from its previous 71.65 bcf per day.
In it short-term outlook, the EIA said natgas wellhead prices for first-quarter 1997 should average $2.51 per thousand cubic feet (mcf), up from its September estimate for the period of $1.92.
Residential gas prices for the first quarter should be $6.29 per mcf, up from the September estimate of $5.79 per mcf, the EIA said.

First-quarter 1997 natgas demand should average 80.72 bcf per day, down from the September estimate of 81.19 bcf per day. But last-quarter December demand was higher than estimated previously at 65.25 bcf per day instead of September's estimate of 62.01 bcf per day, the EIA said, raising the winter season projection.

Natural gas production this winter should average 55.25 bcf per day, compared with September projection of 52.98 bcf. Fourth quarter 1996 production was estimated to have been 10 percent higher than thought previously, it said.

Looking beyond this winter, the EIA said continued economic growth, aided by lower gas prices and recovering West Coast demand, should help boost annual natgas demand in 1997 and 1998 to the highest levels since 1973.
In 1997, it said annual demand should grow by 1.4 percent to 22.55 trillion cubic feet (Tcf), led by growth in electricity generating and industrial sectors.
In 1998, annual demand should reach 23.1 Tcf, up an additional 2.3 percent, the EIA said.
Wellhead prices for 1997 should average $2.09 per mcf, down from 1996's $2.17. In 1998, prices should drop further to $1.98 per mcf.
U.S. dry gas annual production in 1997 should be 19.43 Tcf, up from 1996's 19.05 trillion, and it should rise to 19.85 Tcf in 1998.
Net gas imports, which grew by 2.5 percent in 1996, should increase by 6.9 percent to 2.94 Tcf in 1997 because of strong demand and favorable price differentials, and to 3.18 Tcf in 1998.

In the outlook for this winter heating season, the EIA said natural gas stock withdrawals this winter should average 9.35 bcf per day, considerably below the last projection of 10.2 bcf, as higher production levels meet more of the increased demand.

End of first-quarter 1997 stock levels should be 5.213 Tcf, 2.4 percent higher than projected in September, the EIA said, because of a greater reliance on production, rather than stocks, to meet incremental demand.
Net imports for the winter should average 8.3 bcf per day, lower than the 8.5 bcf forecast in the last outlook because of an estimated drop in fourth-quarter 1996 imports.
The EIA said it boosted winter heating season price and demand projections partly because cold weather increased fourth-quarter 1996 gas use.
